messages.subject: Logistic regressions on simulated data

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Logistic regressions on simulated data
parts:
Do you mean underperforming in the sense of
being slower or underperforming in the sense of
not getting the estimates you expect?

By GLM you mean the R package glm? That's not going
to produce exactly the same estimates because the Stan
model has priors and estimates using posterior mean rather
than posterior mode (which is what I'm assuming glm in R
is doing --- I don't actually know that). So one thing I'd
check is sensitivity to the priors and then I'd do posterior
histograms of the coefficient estimates and see how they
look vs. the glm estimates.

I also saw this on the page you linked:

> I was mostly interested in speeding up the calculation and found that,
> with an equal number of burn-in (warmup) and
> final saved steps, a run that took 54 minutes with JAGS
> took 3.5 minutes with STAN. I do not claim that is a perfectly
> fair or complete comparison. It does include the compile time of the
> C++ code in STAN and 500 adapt steps in JAGS.

Raw time per iteration isn't important, it's time per number
of effective samples. It's a bit hard to do a direct apples-to-apples
comparison because the effective sample size estimators differ
between R2jags and RStan (or Stan's bin/print on the command line).

You probably also want to measure time to convergence (that is, time
before you get your first effective sample).

You might also want to compare memory usage if that matters. The
ratio between Stan and JAGS varies depending on the connectivity of
the graphical model in JAGS.

Here's the linked model:

data {
int<lower=0> nPredictors;
int<lower=0> nData;
int<lower=0,upper=1> y[nData];
matrix[nData,nPredictors] x;
}
parameters {
real z0;
vector[nPredictors] z;
}
model {
z0 ~ normal(0,3.2);
for (d in 1:nPredictors)
z[d] ~ normal(0,2);
for (n in 1:nData)
y[n] ~ bernoulli(inv_logit(z0 + x[n] * z));
}


The model looks like a basic logistic regression with an
intercept.

Using bernoulli_logit (as Andrew suggested) and vectorizing
should make it considerably faster and require less memory.

model {
z0 ~ normal(0,3.2);
z ~ normal(0,2);
y ~ bernoulli_logit(z0 + x * z);
}

Whether you think it's clearer or not will depend on how
you feel about vectorization :-) We named "bernoulli_logit"
the way we did because the parameter is on the logit scale
compared to the usual [0,1] parameter for Bernoulli.

- Bob

You can do it just how you wrote it if z is a matrix or 2D array. If
z is just a vector, then you can just write

z ~ normal(beta * prior, sigma_z);

parts:
Works for me. :-)

Here's my Stan model (which is just vectorized with variable
renaming from what David originally sent):


----------------lr.stan----------------
data {
int<lower=0> K;
int<lower=0> N;
int<lower=0,upper=1> y[N];
matrix[N,K] x;
}
parameters {
real alpha;
vector[K] beta;
}
model {
alpha ~ normal(0,3.2);
beta ~ normal(0,2);
y ~ bernoulli_logit(alpha + x * beta);
}
---------------------------------------

And here's the simulation in R:

-----------------lr.R-----------------------
library('rstan');

inv_logit <- function(u) { return(1 / (1 + exp(-u))); }

N <- 1000;
K <- 4;
x <- matrix(rnorm(N*K, 0, 1.5), N, K);
alpha <- rnorm(1,0,3.2);
beta <- rnorm(K,0,2);
y <- rep(NA,N);
for (n in 1:N)
y[n] <- rbinom(1,1,inv_logit(alpha + sum(x[n,] * beta)));

fit <- stan("lr.stan",data=c("K","N","y","x"));
---------------------------------------

Logistic regression's just noisy. This was with N=1000 cases
and K=4 dimensions (+ intercept) with no correlation among the
predictors x.

If you examine the uncertainty in the posterior in Stan, you'll
see it has pretty high deviation for each parameter.

If you want to compute posterior means yourself, it goes like this:

> mean(fit.ss$beta[,1])
[1] 0.07030561
